speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: JACQUES CARTIER BRIDGE, MONTREAL- ANNOUNCEMENT OF CRIMINAL CHARGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the house would be interested to know that the investigation into possible criminal activities in connection with the collection of tolls on the Jacques Cartier bridge has now advanced to the point where it appears that criminal charges should be laid. Accordingly my colleague, the Minister of Justice, has appointed counsel to assess the evidence now available, to advise as to the course of further criminal investigations, and to draft the charges that should be laid. The house can be assured that the completion of this aspect of the investigation and the laying of charges against all those who may be involved in a criminal way will be pressed with the greatest possible speed.
It is the view of the government that until this aspect of the investigation has been completed, and the number and extent of those involved in criminal activities have been ascertained and specific charges have been laid, the hearings before the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines should not be resumed. As soon, however, as charges have been laid, the government will ask the committee to resume its hearings immediately and make the fullest possible examination of all other aspects of the matter. speechtext:
I wish to address a question to the Minister of National Defence in view of the fact that the United Kingdom has decided to change its plans and revert to manned interceptors, as reported in a news item in the Ottawa Journal of February 19 with a London date line, the first sentence of which reads as follows:
Just three years after the government announced that the end of manned tactical airplanes was in sight plans now are going ahead for new fighters and bombers, both to be operated by flying crews.
Can the minister tell the house whether the government has decided to follow a similar course in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. G. R. Pearkes (Minister of Naiional Defence):
subtopic: REPORTED REVERSION TO USE OF MANNED INTERCEPTORS BY U.K.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as far as I know the defence policy of the United Kingdom, as expressed in the most recent white paper, is to combine the various forms of defence against attack from the air. They are going ahead with the development of ground to air missiles, and at the same time they have some interceptors.
As far as Canada is concerned, we have interceptors at the present time and we are going ahead with the preparations for the Bomarc missile.

speechtext:
I wish to address a question to the Minister of Public Works. In view of the recent decision by Brunswick Mining and Smelting Corporation

Limited to bring the Brunswick lead-zinc mine into commercial production, can the minister advise the house whether the government is now prepared to proceed with major developments in the port of Bathurst, as announced in a communique issued by the Prime Minister on September 27, 1957?

speakeroldname: Hon. D. J. Walker (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subtopic: BATHURST, N.B.  INQUIRY AS TO FEDERAL DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I thank the hon. member for his question, and answer it under the following headings.
First, in 1957 the government, at the request of the Brunswick Mining and Smelting Company, agreed to carry out capital dredging in the entrance channel and turning basin at Carron point at an estimated cost of $3,500,000. This agreement was on the understanding that the Brunswick Mining and Smelting Company would proceed with its plans to invest in excess of $20 million for a lead smelter, zinc concentrator and other facilities, including a dock.
Second, at the request of the company this agreement was suspended due to the depressed condition of the world market in lead and zinc, which made it inadvisable for the company to carry out this development.
Third, the department has received no request from the company for a renewal of this agreement.

speechtext:
The answer to the first part of the question asked by the hon. member is that the Department of National Defence does not exercise control over the activities of service personnel during their off-duty hours as long as their activities do not bring any disrepute to the service, and if there is no emergency.
The second part asks regarding the selling to the general public of automotive and petroleum products. If the hon. member knows of any particular instances where members of the general public have been supplied I shall be only too pleased to look into this and correct it. subtopic: AVAILABILITY OF INFORMATION ON FILES OF CLAIMANTS
speechtext: I wish to address a question to the Minister of Labour. To what persons or organizations, other than labour unions, will the unemployment insurance commission make available information on the files of claimants with the claimants' written, signed approval?

subtopic: AVAILABILITY OF INFORMATION ON FILES OF CLAIMANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member advised me of his intention to ask this question, and I have the following answer for him.
The release of information by officials of the unemployment insurance commission relating to individual claims is specifically dealt with in section 98 of the act. In this section it is set out that such information may be released where the commission deems it advisable, thus leaving discretion in the hands of the commission. The governing factor in all such cases is, of course, the claimant's own interest and his welfare.
In the case of labour unions, where presumably the union is acting on behalf of the claimant, it is presumed to be in the interests of the claimant. There are other cases, even where the request might be made by the claimant, where such a presumption would not exist. There are no definite categories of persons or groups to whom such information is or is not released.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that each case is dealt with on its merits by the officials of the commission, keeping in mind the central factor of the claimant's welfare. I might add that if the hon. member has any specific case of an individual or organization in mind, if he would bring it to my attention I should be glad to look into it.

Mr. Chairman, this item deals with the municipal incentive program, and the amount of the item is $15 million. It is an estimate and the government is prepared, as I have mentioned, to increase this amount by as much as is necessary, depending upon submissions by the municipalities of the various projects that come within the scope of this plan.
When we started this debate, Mr. Chairman, according to your ruling it was to be kept within the scope of this item. However, with the agreement of the house it has taken a wider scope, and we are now discussing the problem of unemployment as a whole. The release of the statistics by the dominion bureau of statistics last week brought about the concern exhibited by all members in this house; consequently the debate has ranged around that release. I want to say that there have been some constructive suggestions from those who have taken part in the debate, suggestions that need closer scrutiny by the government. However, in the main there has been criticism of what is being done at the present time, and the suggestion that more should be done.
It is acknowledged by the government that this particular program is not the complete solution of the problem. There is no question about that. This government has acknowledged the problem of unemployment in this country and has endeavoured to do something about it in the past through various means, and we are trying to do something in the present situation.
The dominion bureau of statistics publication, to which reference has been made, has other aspects to it. It is not one that is entirely devoted to the stark side of the picture. The dominion bureau of statistics release summarizes the employment situation as of mid-January, 1960. It shows that our labour force totals 6,203,000, which compared with the labour force in January, 1959 shows an increase of 127,000. The number of persons with jobs in January, 1960, according to this latest release, is estimated at 5,699,000, which compared with January, 1959 shows an increase of 161,000. This means, Mr. Chairman, that there are 161,000 more Canadians at work this year than at the same time last year.
Those without jobs and seeking work, in January, 1960 are shown at 504,000. This is 34,000 less than in January, 1959, and this 79951-0-891
Supply-Labour
figure for January, 1959 is below the figure for January, 1958. The sharpest shift in seasonal activities takes place from December to January, and that has been the case each and every year. The amount of the increase in unemployment depends upon two developments, Mr. Chairman; first, the amount of the seasonal decline in employment and, second, the seasonal reduction of the labour force.
These statistics, as released by the dominion bureau, show that an estimated 40,000 fewer men and 6,000 more woman were looking for work in January this year than the year before. On the employment side, we have 86,000 more men and 75,000 more women who have jobs, so that total employment is up 2.6 per cent from a year earlier.
It is well known-and there is no attempt at this time on my part to minimize this problem of unemployment-that a large number of either the single or married seekers of work come from families where one or more member is already employed. This means that unemployment should not be equated with total loss of income in each of these family units. In order to illustrate this, I would say that of the 504,000 in January, 1960 who are classified as without jobs and seeking work, an estimated 237,000 were single people. If we break this figure down we find that it represents some 187,000 men and 50,000 women; and of the 504,000, 267,000 were married. This figure represents 253,000 men and 14,000 women.
As I mentioned before, and I want to emphasize, unemployment is a serious problem. This government recognized it when it assumed office in 1957. Now, what did we do about this problem at that time? Recognizing that it could become a lot worse than it is at the present time, this government took certain steps to alleviate the situation. First of all we slowed down

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: I wonder if the minister would permit a question.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: Did he say that when his government took office unemployment was much worse than it is at the present time?

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext:
No, I did not say that at all. I said if we had not taken certain action then it could have been much worse than it is at the present time.
What did we do? We slowed down the rate of immigration. Slowing down immigration is not a step that any government wishes to take. We all realize that immigration is necessary. We have a very large country, and immigration helps to increase our consumer purchasing power which, in turn, provides opportunities for more employment. However

Supply-Labour
in a situation where people are allowed to come into the country and who are kept in the dispersement centres, as they were just prior to 1957, without any jobs for as long as one year, something must be done. This is certainly not good housekeeping. We slowed down immigration in order to give the economy an opportunity to absorb those who were coming into this country. This had quite an effect.
Housing was stimulated. No one can say that the action taken by the government in housing was not necessary or did not prove effective, because housing in this country probably supplies more employment than any other undertaking that could be stimulated by the government. Public works were stepped up in order to help those who might find themselves without employment. Then we extended the unemployment insurance benefits by an additional two months in the seasonal class. Last session the regular benefits were extended to 52 weeks. Certain large projects were undertaken, such as the Saskatchewan dam and power developments in the maritimes. Deficit budgeting was brought about in order to stimulate employment.
These are some of the things this government endeavoured to do. These things indicate that there was some willingness on the part of this government to face up to this situation and to see what they could do to alleviate it. There were many other things done that I will not dwell upon at this time.
There has been a great deal of talk to the effect that unemployment is something that has just happened recently. That it is something that has been brought about since the Conservative government came into office. Let us look at the picture; let us go back and look at what the dominion bureau of statistics figures show.
At this point I might say I am very glad that some attention is being paid to the dominion bureau of statistics releases in this regard.
It is not my intention to cast any reflection upon any member of this house but I want to make some remarks about the attitude of the hon. member for Essex East. As an example, I watched him with a great deal of interest just a few weeks ago when he was on television and I found, to my great surprise, that he stated that he always thought that the dominion bureau of statistics figure was the proper figure for measuring unemployment in Canada, but that since he has been in the opposition he has had more opportunity and more time to review the whole situation and has come to the conclusion-and also some of his colleagues; I do

not think they all have; I am quite certain of that, but some of his group have done so- that this figure of the dominion bureau of statistics is not any good at all and that the N.E.S. figure is now the right one.
What that really means is that Right Hon. Mr. Howe and my predecessor, Mr. Gregg, must have been wrong about these things because they asserted that was the right figure. Of course, if you want to go back and look at the standards set up by the International Labour Organization at Geneva which established this formula for unemployment, they must be wrong also. The United States, which adopted that formula from the I.L.O. and which use it as a measure of unemployment in that country, must be wrong also. Of course Mr. Howe and the former Liberal government must have been wrong also because we now have a different attitude toward the measure of unemployment in this country.

speechtext:
I wonder whether the

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: Will the minister tell us when he saw the light on the road to Damascus because he always used the N.E.S. figure when he was over here on this side of the house.

speechtext: I will be quite frank, Mr. Chairman. I came to this house in 1952. I had no experience in the house at all. When I came into the picture in 1954 and 1955, I must be frank with you and say I did not realize which figure was the official figure.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER

That is a big job
in itself.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: Let us look at the situation back in 1936 when the hon. member and his government were in office. I am not going to look at any figures released by the dominion bureau of statistics for a time when unemployment is at its peak, which is in February or March. Let us look at the figure in June.

speechtext:
Take the whole

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: The figure for the whole year would not be a great deal of use before 1936. In June employment in Canada is usually at its highest or at least it is on its way up to its highest peak. That is not really the month when unemployment is at its lowest. This date I am going to give is for June and it is taken from the D.B.S. reference paper No. 23, revised edition. In 1936 the figure for those unemployed was 12.8 per cent of the total labour force.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: May I ask the minister whether these figures were arrived at in precisely the same way by the same sampling methods as the figure was arrived at in the 40's and 50's?

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: I would presume that the same method is used by the dominion bureau of statistics in ah cases. This is a D.B.S. release.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext:
No. I asked them what the percentage was of the labour force of those unemployed during that time and this is the figure they gave me.
In 1938 the figure was 11.4 per cent of the labour force which was unemployed. In 1939, again it was 11.4 per cent. In 1940, even after the world war started-and it started in the fall of 1939-it was still 9.2 per cent. Then they said, "Now we have a solution for unemployment; there is a war on and everybody goes to work". In 1941 the figure dropped to 4.4 per cent. That is the story. That is the way unemployment was. When you talk about the Liberal party being the good times party, with no unemployment, may I say that here is a clear picture of what was happening for the first six years they were in office.
This government has been in office only since June, 1957 and this is a cycle that has been going on for all these years. They say, "Why have you not done something about it? Why have you not eliminated this problem?" But as I said in the early part of
Supply-Labour
my remarks, this government recognized this situation and we did not just look at the picture. We have tried to do something about it through these various things that I have pointed out and many other things.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: Will the minister permit a question?

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: Will he explain how this government has concentrated upon particular areas that are suffering most? What I mean is this. We have appreciated what he has asserted in his outline of general policy. What about the areas such as the one I represent where we have winter unemployment ranging up to 22 per cent and 25 per cent of the labour force. That is the situation right now, over 20 per cent out of work. What is your particular policy there?

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: We have looked at that situation and I must say this. I am extremely proud of some of the attempts that have been made in that area. When Canadian Car threatened to move out, this government was instrumental in holding them there and they are still operating there.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: At its most stable time the working force was in the neighbourhood of 1,000. It is now about 250. The company is holding there but that is quite a cut-down.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext:
That is quite true. Of course, that is the business of the company, as to the amount of business they may have there. But let me also say that the hon. member has a peculiar area there in that a great many people are employed as woodsmen. As an example, I talked to some of the people not in Port Arthur but in the neighbouring city of Fort William. One gentleman told me he has never worked during the wintertime in 12 winters. I asked him why. He said he was employed as a bush worker and in that particular summer made $7,000. When I asked him what he was doing in the wintertime, what he was doing then, he said "nothing". I said, "That is too bad". He said, "It is not too bad. I am drawing unemployment insurance". I do not know how many people there are to whom this situation applies, but this is just one example that I ran up against when I was in his area. If the hon. member has any suggestions about how to alleviate that situation in his area, I shall be only too glad to look into it and to do everything in my power to implement it, provided that it is a reasonable suggestion.
As to 1946, we will come in this instance to the present part of the year. In March, 1946, 4.7 per cent of the labour force was unemployed.

Supply-Labour

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: What month is that?

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: March.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: One month?

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: That is right. That is what we are dealing with. We are dealing with the release for January this year. We are dealing with one month also. In March, 1947, the figure was 3 per cent; in 1948 it was 3.2 per cent. I am not just quoting large figures. I want to give the complete picture year by year.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: In 1949 the figure was 4 per cent. In 1950 it jumped to 6.1 per cent. Of course, the Korean war came along then and it was another solution to unemployment. During all this time there is no evidence whatsoever of any action on the part of the government of which the hon. member was a distinguished member on the treasury benches.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: Thank you.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext:
There was no action. They waited for one war and then they waited for another war. In 1951 the figure was 3.3 per cent; in 1952, 4 per cent; in 1953, 3.4 per cent; in 1954, 6.1 per cent-the cycle had started again-in 1955, 7.4 per cent; in 1956 it dropped back to 5.3 per cent; and in 1957 it was again 6 per cent.
I am not going to be critical of any individual member, particularly the hon. member for Essex East.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: Oh, why not?

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext:
You can see this has not all been full employment in any one year right down through the list from 1936. It is a thing which has recurred, but it provides evidence that there was no action on the part of the government to do anything about it.
Now we are criticized because it is alleged we are doing nothing about it. We have introduced measures which have not been undertaken before. This municipal incentive program has never been undertaken before; it is something new. I admit immediately it does not solve the problem. The hon. member for Essex East says it is peanuts.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: I said it is anemic.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: Anemic. My hon. friend from As-siniboia said it was peanuts. It may be peanuts to my plump, well fed friends in the opposition-

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: Look at your well fed friends around you.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: -but let me say it is not peanuts to some 40,000 Canadians who will get jobs under this program. To the 40,000 Canadians who will get jobs under this program it means bread and butter on the table.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: How many pounds of butter?

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: How many days?

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: And what kind of bread?

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: The hon. member for Essex East says, how many days. It means approximately 1,578,128 man days of work.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: About four days apiece.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, last year the average was 45 days for each man. Remember, this is during a period of seasonal unemployment, and most of the people are very glad to get the jobs. It is an indication that this government is willing to do something about it. We are willing to listen to any reasonable suggestions which hon. members have.
I would like to commend the hon. member for Kootenay West. He was very reasonable in his contribution to this debate and he gave some suggestions which I think should be looked at very closely. I have always maintained this position, that we, as the federal government, are prepared to recognize, and are recognizing, the unemployment situation as such, but it is not something which the government itself can remedy entirely. We can initiate certain things to help relieve the situation, but it certainly needs the cooperation of hon. members opposite, the cooperation of the provinces, the co-operation of the municipalities and all other interested bodies in this country. Their suggestions, with that co-operation, will help to alleviate to quite a degree the seasonal unemployment we experience in this country.
The hon. member for Essex East made some suggestions about what should be done and he projected a program of ten points. These ten points I have studied closely. Upon their immediate presentation it looked as though there might be something in them, but if his suggestions were implemented, no good could be brought about at once. He recommended in his ten points, three committees and two conferences. I must say at once that, in my opinion, no unemployment has ever been solved in this country through conferences.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: That is what the hon. minister recommended himself; a dominion-provincial conference and a parliamentary committee.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: I did?

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: Your party, and you supported it.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext:
I said earlier when a similar question was posed to me by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that I speak for myself in this regard. What has been said by others in the past is their own responsibility. They were speaking as individual members of this house, and if the hon. member for Essex East has a different viewpoint now than he had when he was sitting on the treasury benches, then he has every right to it.
The hon. member says that this problem is too big for the Minister of Labour to handle by himself. I have never pretended, neither has the government, that the Minister of Labour was responsible for the solving of unemployment in this country, because the actions which have been taken have not been actions taken under the direction of the Minister of Labour but actions taken by the government. In this regard the government does take the responsibility for those actions and future actions which may be taken. I, as Minister of Labour, am naturally the one responsible to the house in respect of these policies.
Another suggestion was made that an advisory board should be set up. I must say that that is true to form because there have been so many advisory boards in the past when the opposition was sitting on the treasury benches that they even had advisory boards to the advisory boards. I suppose the hon. member for Essex East knows that there is an advisory committee on national employment in Canada which was organized in 1941. He is suggesting we organize one now.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: A different kind of thing altogether. The minister has not understood it.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext:
It would not perform any different functions from the one it is performing now in advising the unemployment insurance commission on the situation of unemployment in this country.
Then the hon. member recommended a parliamentary committee. We have a parliamentary committee; it is sitting right now. This is the third day, and there has been every opportunity for reasonable suggestions to come forward. What has the hon. member got in mind as far as a parliamentary committee is concerned? Is it to provide a method of talking about the question? Talking will not solve the problem. We have the opportunity here and now to put forward suggestions, and we have the same function and flexibility as any committee. As a matter of fact, I think this committee has a greater flexibility.
Supply-Labour
Then the hon. member wants a federal-provincial conference. We realize that such a conference may have some use, and we did call one. We wasted no time and called one in July 1958, and not only was it composed of the federal government and the provincial governments, but also the municipal governments, labour bodies, industrial bodies* the Canadian Manufacturers Association and all the most interested people in this country came along to the conference. They had no direction but they sat and discussed the whole problem and made recommendations on incentives, and some of those recommendations have been implemented. In fact, we have before us one of the results of those recommendations.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: I wonder if the minister would permit a question. Could he give us a list of the recommendations of that conference and indicate which of them have been carried out?

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the report of that conference was tabled in this house and is available. All the hon. member has to do is to look at it, and if he feels there is something in that report that the government has not implemented which they should implement, most certainly he can bring it to our attention.
The hon. member also pointed out in the course of his ten points which he said would help unemployment-I have dealt with some of them-that the Canadian Labour Congress has asked for a conference of labour and management on unemployment. That is not so because he referred in particular to a speech which the president of the Canadian Labour Congress made to the board of trade in Toronto, and he requested a conference between labour and management on better labour-management relations, something similar to what is being asked for in the United States by Mr. Meany.

Supply-Labour
The hon. member wants a national employment committee. There is one already in existence. He wants a modification of the winter works plan. He calls this plan anaemic. That is what he called it. Probably it does not take in the whole picture of unemployment but, as I said, it was never intended to; it is just another part of the total effort- a good suggestion which has been put into effect and which has put another 40,000 people to work. Who would not wish to have this program in effect at the present time? As to modifications, what modifications does the hon. member want? Why does he not tell us?

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: As recommended by the Windsor city council.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: A recommendation by one municipality does not apply to all municipalities. It does not follow that all municipalities will be engaged in similar undertakings. The projects vary and there has to be a plan which will give the best opportunity to the majority.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: Or the recommendations made by Mr. George Moody on behalf of the Canadian association of municipalities.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext:
There have been some suggestions that we should pay increased attention to vocational training. I think the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate mentioned this subject during the debate. I should point out, though, that in accordance with the way in which this is now set up, the initiative is in the hands of the provinces. I have personally written to various provinces pointing out that we are prepared to participate in this plan. For example-and I think this might be of interest to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate-on my visit to Bell Island I was asked by the unions there to make provision for a training school on the island because, they said, the people of the island were not prone to go to the mainland to attend training schools. On my return I immediately wrote to the premier of Newfoundland saying that the federal government was prepared to participate in such a plan. They are studying the question in Newfoundland, but to date, we have not heard of a definite commitment. We have taken action in other cases, too, but as I explained, the initiative lies with the provinces.
Last year the number of men taking advantage of vocational training rose by 35 per cent, but that is not enough, because we are only dealing with 3,000 to 5,000 people. We want to participate in measures

providing for the training of a great many more. We want to be able to say we are training people at the rate of 20,000 or 30,000 a year, and we are prepared to do that. However, this necessarily means initiative by the provinces and provincial participation.
Suggestions have been made about setting up a capital assistance fund for the Atlantic provinces. On taking office, this government immediately recognized the necessity of doing something to improve the standard of living in the Atlantic provinces. I need not recite here what action has been taken but we have certainly endeavoured to do all we can in that respect. It is not my intention to take up much more time, Mr. Chairman, but surely we have before us now an estimate of $15 million-and this is not the ceiling. If more work is undertaken we are prepared to go beyond this figure. We can come back here and ask for another $10 or $15 million.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: Can the minister suggest what kind of work can be done under 13 or 14 feet of snow in western Ontario?

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: We are not trying to kid anyone. The municipalities asked for this program. The Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities, including mayors from Saskatoon and Winnipeg where there is snow and where there is frost, asked us to help carry out sewage programs and so on. They said: yes, we can do it. It costs a little more, but if the federal government pays part of the cost of putting these services in we are prepared to go ahead. Since then they have had nothing but the highest praise for this program.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext: Does that reply mean that the present system will continue until we get another request from the municipalities for some improvement?

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext:
We discussed this with the Canadian mayors and municipalities and we told them that because they had seasonal unemployment we were prepared to help them, and they said that some program such as this would be agreeable. If there is snow, then there are other types of work which municipalities can undertake-clearing rights of way, getting out the brush and other projects where there is a large labour content. This is a very acceptable type of program.
Let us see what the municipalities are doing by way of co-operation. The municipalities realize that they must put to work as many people as they can, and they review these projects and sort them out accordingly. The result is that of 1,900 projects amounting in cost to some $84 million the labour content is averaging 35.3 per cent. I think

that is good housekeeping by the municipalities. When they are able to do that I think they are using good common sense. They are choosing projects on which they can employ the higher percentage of labour and from which they can obtain the maximum amount of help in this situation.
There is on the order paper now in the name of the Minister of Public Works a resolution to make more money available for housing. This, too, will be the means of providing employment. I say to hon. members of this house: I welcome your co-operation and I welcome your suggestions but I do hope we can go on to approve this item as well as the item concerned with housing in order that we may put these measures into effect and get the people to work.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext:
Might I ask a question? I did not wish to interrupt the minister in the course of his remarks. During his presentation, the hon. gentleman made the statement, quite properly, that housing creates employment. I think all hon. members will agree with that statement. As the minister knows, the average number of starts for the past five years has been 138,000. Last year housing starts were down as compared with the previous year and the government's objective is apparently 125,000 starts to be made this year. Does the minister think that in view of the present serious unemployment situation there is any justification for the government persisting in its policy of curtailing house construction?

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have just heard the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) try for a few minutes to prove that things are not as bad as we on this side of the house claim them to be. He attempted, by going back to the past, to prove to the country that under the Liberal administration the situation was worse than it is now. The minister said-and I took down his exact words-"If no definite action had been taken, unemployment would be more serious that it is now".
I think the minister should have said: If we had taken definite action, unemployment would not be as serious as it is today. In fact, Mr. Chairman, we are now faced with a situation that reflects no great credit either on the person in charge of the Department of Labour, or on the one entrusted with the future of this country.
The Minister of Labour said, a while ago, that "talking will not solve the problem".
Supply-Labour
Perhaps, but unemployment will certainly not be solved either by voting $15 million to assist municipalities in carrying out winter work.
The minister said that not all municipalities took advantage of this plan, but that they are entitled, and are given an opportunity, to participate.

X should like through you, Mr. Chairman, to remind my hon. friends in the Liberal party that under the Conservative government unemployment insurance benefits have been extended to married women and fishermen, and there has been an extension to 52 weeks of the period during which benefits are given to unemployed workers.

Actually, there were so many of them that they come from all quarters.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few remarks to make on this item, one reason being that earlier in this debate I had the dubious distinction of being mentioned in the Pickersgill papers. Therefore for that and other reasons I am speaking in this debate. It was brought out during the debate, which has gone on for some time, that the unemployment figures in my area were very bad. First of all, before I go on I should like to congratulate the Minister of Labour for the winter works program which has been initiated by him and the government. I should also like to thank him for the speedy action which was taken, while I was at home before the start of the present session, with respect to a large number of unemployment insurance claims that were held up in the regional office in Moncton. Following a telephone call from one of the executives of the united steelworkers union I immediately called the minister's office in Ottawa and as a result things were moving within an hour and a half and the claims were being looked after properly as they should have been.
With respect to unemployment in the county of Pictou I should first like to outline briefly the reasons for unemployment there as I see them. I think the situation should be explained. For many years up to 1951 coal mining was our most important industry, employing approximately 2,000 men. In the year 1951 our coal mines commenced to close. First the Allan shaft closed in 1951 followed in rapid succession in subsequent years by the MacGregor mine in February 1957 and Albion mine and also a substantial curtailment of work at the Drummond mine in Westville. As a result, employment afforded coal miners in that area has decreased from approximately
2,000	workers to approximately 500 at the present time.
This all came about before I became the member for the riding and before the present government came into power. As I said, the result has been a great decrease in the number of men employed by the coal mines and as a result we have had a labour surplus on our hands since that time. We have a number of other types of industry there including fishing and farming and small industries

making bricks, tile, structural steel and so on but the plants carrying out the work are not large enough to take the surplus labour force and therefore we have been faced with this situation.
Mention was made by the hon. member for Gloucester of the unemployment situation in connection with the Eastern Car Company plant in Trenton which, since the closing of our coal mines, has become the largest employer in that area. The Canadian National and Canadian Pacific railways are the largest purchasers of railway cars, freight cars from the Eastern Car plant. They also make purchases from the National Steel Car Company in Hamilton, and Canada Car in Montreal. We were told, after the last order Eastern Car received from the Canadian National for a special type of box car, that the railway had not made up its budget for the year 1960 so no further orders would be forthcoming until the budget had been looked into. In addition, Canadian Pacific railway had not decided what they would need in the way of rolling stock for the coming year.
I should like to point out to the minister something which was pointed out in the excerpt from the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, February 9 of this year, which was read in part by the hon. member for Gloucester. This article concerns a submission by the Pictou county ministerial association, and I should like to read a few words which were uttered by the Rev. Mr. Kingsbury, of the Anglican church in the town of Stellarton, who has long been a great worker on that committee in the area:
Mr. Kingsbury said the clergy was involved in the situation as much as the men who carry the lunch pails. He said men working in the car works in Trenton were usually employed for only five or six months each year. He suggested the governments be asked to provide work at the plants in the time of the most need-in the winter months. Although the full year was important, he said the winter was the time when men should be taking home the pay cheques.
This matter was brought to my attention shortly after I returned to Ottawa, but had been mentioned to me before that. This plant is the largest employer in the county and its history, except in wartime, has not been one of permanent employment. 1 would agree with this suggestion by the Rev. Mr. Kingsbury, and ask that work be provided in the winter months. This would make one of the best winter projects possible. I might add that the united steelworkers of America, local 1231, wrote a letter to the Minister of Transport in connection with this matter, the sentiments of which I endorse. The letter, in part, reads:
Again we would like to point out the necessity of arranging railway car building programs in the winter months. It seems that our plants are always
Supply-Labour
idle in the winter. You appreciate that if the plants worked in the winter and were idle in the summer most of the hardships would disappear as the average citizen can find something in the summer when many work programs are being carried on, and if he has to be idle it takes far less to keep him going when no fuel, winter clothing, etc., are required.
Another matter which was brought out by the union in connection with this winter work, and which is an interesting point, is that one of the industries in this area, Standard Clay Products, for years worked in the summer and closed during the winter. However, some two or three years ago the company was taken over by a holding company which immediately reversed the work schedule from summer to winter, after they found out that it was necessary to maintain the plant in the winter with heat and power.
I should like to bring again to the attention of the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Labour at this time, the fact that the government should submit to the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific, the largest purchasers of this type of rolling stock, the necessity for giving orders for rolling stock during the winter months.
Amongst other things, the hon. member for Gloucester brought out the fact that the ministerial association suggested that the government should proceed with public projects, such as the federal building in New Glasgow. It is about 10 years since this project has been mooted, and the former government was unable to decide on a site for it. I am glad to say that the site has been cleared and I hope that within another week, or two weeks at the most, tenders will be called for this federal building. This project will provide a lot of work in the area and the building is a necessity so far as the town of New Glasgow is concerned.
The hon. member for Gloucester also quoted from the same press clipping some words of the Rev. Father Chisholm. Father Chisholm has long been an outstanding leader in the community, and I should like to quote some remarks of his in order to give the hon. member some food for thought. I quote:
Father Chisholm said it was up to the clergy to get behind the common man because "they are the producers of the nation's wealth." He said Pictou county and the maritimes as a whole needed a united voice at Ottawa.
"We have been playing party politics too long. We must get together and speak as one voice to solve our problem."
I commend that thought to the hon. member for Gloucester. The hon. member also stated that conditions in the county of Pictou were similar to those which existed in many other areas in the Atlantic provinces. I do not agree with that at all. The other areas, such as the Halifax area, the Saint John area, the

Supply-Labour
riding of the hon. member for Queens-Lunen-burg where the Mersey Paper Company is starting to construct a $3.5 million addition to their mill, have different conditions. In many other places in the Atlantic provinces, things are very definitely progressing. I do not intend to read it in toto, but I have here a clipping from the Montreal Gazette of February 19, 1960, which is headed, "$100 Million Building Program Set for Nova Scotia".
Among other things, it says that two areas, Halifax and the strait of Canso, will get the major share of the work. There is a $40 million sulphite mill for Nova Scotia Pulp Limited at Point Tupper; over $6 million for an international airport at Kelly Lake; construction at Dalhousie University; additions to both the Lord Nelson and Nova Scotian hotels; some $4 million for new married quarters at Greenwood; $2 million for a shopping centre at Sydney and $1 million for a new hospital at Waterford. I think, therefore, the situation in the county I represent is extraordinary. It is definitely different from the situation in other areas. 1 would recommend to this government that a committee or some other mode of investigation be set up at once. This committee should be composed of federal, provincial, municipal, industrial and labour leaders in the area and should fully investigate conditions throughout the country.
As I have said, the reason I am suggesting this is because conditions in this constituency are unlike those in most parts of Canada and in other parts of the Atlantic provinces where industry is booming and things are really going ahead. I believe that such an investigation should be held because it could look into the matter of industry in the upper towns which include Trenton, Stellarton, New Glasgow, Westville and the town of Pictou. I believe this investigation could bring forth some ideas on how industry could be diversified in the area. Just recently a half million dollar contract has been let to the Trenton works of the Dominion Steel and Coal Company for parts for electronic equipment. This is part of a general contract which has gone to the E. M. I. Cosser Ltd. in the Halifax area. This is the type of thing which could be carried out in these plants which are made up of the Trenton Steel Works and the Eastern Car Company, which I have already stated make railway cars, and Trenton Industries Limited, which is one of the finest machine shops in Canada. I have gone through these shops and very definitely they could carry out the best type of work.
The Nova Scotia government has taken steps in introducing the Faini Company, a textile plant in Stellarton which is another

form of diversification. I will therefore say that definitely there are other forms of industry which could be obtained for this county, things which could be done in present plants and other industries which could be brought forward in connection with the Industrial Estates Limited of Nova Scotia, and things which could be done by the federal government.

Trenton Steel Works Limited, which make axles for cars in Canada, have, as I understand it, 230 men employed at this time and Trenton Industries Limited have 190. Something which has been done in a matter the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska brought forward in his speech last week regarding various things set out by the Atlantic members, among them the promise of cheap power. I believe that the new grid set-up between the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick will assist in this way. Finally, as to the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate, may I just say that as far as the county of Pictou is concerned, I was born there, brought up there and received my education in the town of Westville, a small coal mining town. I worked in the mines there during the summer holidays, just as a great many other members have worked in various places. In setting up my law office there, back in the years when the Drummond Coal Company threatened to close, I recall that delegates were sent to Ottawa here as well as to Halifax. I do not know whether the hon. member was whittling willows, sharpening pencils or sitting in the seats of the mighty on the treasury benches at that time but I will tell him this. The reception obtained by that delegation did no good. I do not know fully how they were treated but certainly nothing was done and the mine finally was carried on with 100 men instead of 500. That is one reason for the number of unemployed, miners especially. But I would say to him that

as long as I am a member, or no matter where I am, I owe a duty to this county; and there is no doubt that I will speak up for it, whether in this house or elsewhere.

Mr. Chairman, an opposition is certainly a good thing in this parliament, because it enables us to know what happens in Canada, and to find out that there are more than three quarters of a million unemployed in this country. We did not hear hon. members on the government benches speak about it,	except, perhaps, one of them,	my hon. friend
from Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Van Horne) who realizes that there are unemployed people seeking work in this country.
A few moments ago we listened with much interest to the speech of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr). However, he was, to my mind, not in order, as we are discussing the winter works program to help the unemployed, while he spoke all the time of the hundreds of thousands who were employed. He suggested that, if there were more people working in Canada, it was due to this government. On the other hand, he said that the former administration was responsible for the present number of unemployed.
As a matter of fact, he was not the only one to say so. Whenever things go wrong in this country, Conservatives blame the Liberals and the former governments. However, when everything goes well, thanks to some legislation introduced by the Liberal party, they claim credit for it, and reap acclaim for such legislation, which they pretend to have worked out themselves.
Now, as far as wet blankets are concerned, as the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) would say, there is none better than this government, including the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot. This government brags that it has done more in three years than we did in twenty two. As a matter of fact, they succeeded in spreading many more wet blankets in two years than we did in twenty two.
The proof, Mr. Chairman, is that nobody cares about present conditions. I have now in hand a copy of the speech from the throne reproduced on three columns or so, or one and a half pages. In the speech from the throne, I find five words with regard to unemployment. And do you know what it says about unemployment? I quote:
The recurrent problem of seasonal unemployment remains, however, but apart from this ... etc.
It is like the song "All is well, madame la marquise, all is very well"!
Supply-Labour
There is of some mention of the independence of Nigeria, of an impending meeting of great heads of states, of scholarships for commonwealth students who are coming over here to study; and of various other matters which, though they are doubtlessly most interesting, hardly give the unemployed anything to eat nor, indeed, any work. And that is the reason why I submit that this government is ignoring this problem which, in my opinion, is the most important of all.
Astounding figures are quoted, huge sums of money-$15 million-are voted to help the unemployed, while last year, under that famous municipal winter works incentive program for 1958-1959, two thirds only of the $10 million provided were used. This means that there still remains $3J million which the municipalities did not utilize.
And now, a new program is being submitted by the government and we are invited to vote $15 million. But why not, $20 million or $25 million? It is a well known fact that the Conservatives are quite prone to quoting impressive figures as window dressing. Fifty million could have been mentioned. The government knows perfectly that, in the spring, there will remain practically half or perhaps a third of that amount. But, to come back to that famous program, I have here a copy of it, which is more explicit than the law itself, because it is full of conditions which are practically impossible to fulfill and which do not affect, or very slightly, those people who are really in need of work. That program is in the form of a letter addressed by the Minister of Labour. His main purpose is to encourage municipalities to increase job opportunities. Do you know what that incentive program amounts to? It represents from 6 to 12 per cent of the total cost of works. I quote:
We trust that this program, added to other efforts made by governments-
The other governments. Do you know, Mr. Chairman, what is the effort being made by the Ontario government? Nothing at all, Mr. Chairman, nothing. And the effort made by the Ontario government? Twenty five per cent of salaries.
And the letter goes on to say:
"We trust that this program will encourage industry and individuals".
Do you know in what way it will encourage industry and individuals? First of all, that money was collected through that famous conversion loan. Besides, industries and individuals cannot obtain money any more, because the government has taken it over to pay its debts.

Supply-Labour
When industries are in need of money for expansion purposes, they have to borrow; and if they can, they have to do so at exorbitant rates.
Is that, Mr. Chairman, the way of encouraging industry and individuals?
I have here, Mr. Chairman, a newspaper item which reads:
Credit restrictions, as well as irresponsibility have resulted in an increase of 50 per cent of bankruptcies in the province of Quebec.
How can you expect these people to contribute to the solution of unemployment? It is not I who say so, it is the protonotary.
This increase of close to 50 per cent is due first of all to the credit restrictions that were in effect last year.
That is a fine way to help the unemployed.
On the other hand, municipalities are being asked to undertake works that may not be urgent, that could be put off till next year. But the government forgets, on the other hand, that they have to pay more than 85 per cent of the costs of this program. The municipalities are forced to borrow money at rates varying from 7 to 7-J per cent.
I have, Mr. Chairman, a newspaper clipping of March 4, 1959, saying the city of Montreal had submitted 41 projects which cost it $2,007,000. Do you know what was the federal government's share in the cost of those projects?
It was $243,000, Mr. Chairman; in other words 12 per cent.
In order to obtain $243,000, the city of Montreal is forced to borrow $2 million at 7J per cent. Should those works be put off until a year from now, the city of Montreal would be forced to pay 7J per cent for two years, that is $300,000.
Therefore, in order to obtain $243,000 from the federal government, the municipality is forced to spend $300,000 needlessly, not including the $2 million which are tied up forever.
This year, the same proposal is offered.
Let us take, for instance, the province of Quebec where this year, there are 243,384 unemployed. The city of Montreal itself has 40 per cent of that number.
Have you heard the province of Quebec complain about having one third of the country's unemployed? This afternoon the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) asked this question of the Minister of Labour:
Will the minister tell the house if he has received any communication from the authorities of the province of Quebec expressing their concern at the unemployment situation in the province of Quebec and suggesting a possible program for Its solution?

Unemployment is not important.
Yet in 1959, a church leader, His Eminence Cardinal Leger, made this statement:
On the other hand, it is a responsibility of the state to play a positive part and do its full share. Despite all their ingenuity, individuals and organizations cannot alone cope with the unemployment problem. Public bodies have a duty, as was indicated by Pius XII, to provide the greatest possible measure of employment by undertaking generally useful works and by making jobs easier to get.
That is the position of church authorities. How does the province of Quebec respond to that call, which is all at once logical, human and based on common sense?
Municipalities have to pay, out of their own resources, over 85 per cent of the cost of whatever works they may undertake to deal with unemployment.
There is an act which is entitled the Unemployment Assistance Act, to help the unemployed who are ineligible for unemployment insurance benefits.
Mr. Chairman, do you know what has been the share of the province of Quebec out of the amounts paid out by Ottawa? Not one cent, Mr. Chairman, absolutely nothing.
In these winter works programs, there are some jobs to be undertaken by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton). Those jobs involve building access roads to the forests and developing camp sites.
Such expenditures existed under the Liberals. Out of $6 million that were spent by Ottawa to develop 500 camp sites, how much do you think the province of Quebec has received? Not one penny.
