There has been a lightning exchange across the floor which has probably altered the course of the debate a little bit and probably has given us a little rest from some of the problems under debate. I am sure the minister will appreciate it. I was interested in hearing the previous speaker being queried by the minister as to whether
Supply-Labour
or not the winter works program was of any value. I would suggest that the winter works program has been of some value to some parts of Canada, but it has been of no value to other parts of Canada. The winter works program should fit into the unemployment picture in general.
I believe it has been generally agreed that if three quarters of a million people are looking for work, then we have a very serious problem. While the minister is correct in saying that there are more people employed now than there were a year ago, he should also take into consideration that the population has increased and obviously there should be more people employed. We have an annual population growth in Canada of well over 2 per cent per year. This will be reflected in the labour figures, just as they will in other statistics. The fact that three quarters of a million people are looking for work is certainly an indication that this government must give more consideration to the matter of full employment. We must, in Canada, be adult enough to be able to supply our people with work.
The Canadian situation has not appeared to be so serious in the last two or three years because you can walk down the street at the height of the unemployment period and you will not find any number of people standing around as you did during the depression. I have noticed in my travels that there are not nearly the number of people around railroad stations as there used to be. I think we have done something through legislation to alleviate some of the problems that unemployment produces.
Unemployment insurance is a good example of what we have been able to do, what the Canadian people have been able to do, to alleviate some of the problems produced by unemployment. The workers and employers contribute to this plan, and they have been able to take care of some of their own unemployment problems.
Second, I think there has been an increase in part-time employment. People who are employed in bush operations quite often drive taxis or go to work in service stations or do other types of jobs on a part-time basis. This means that they are not on relief. It means in many cases that they are able to stay in the communities in which they have lived; they are able to get by, and still, at the same time should be classed as unemployed persons.
The seasonal benefits that are obtainable in some industries have been taken into consideration in negotiations with the unions that are bargaining in those industries. There has been consideration of the fact that these men are going to be employed for only part

Supply-Labour
of the year, and the unions have succeeded in getting them enough money that they can carry over the period of unemployment. In this way the man does not become a liability on the community by requesting relief from the municipality.
The winter works program has been a step in this direction. In the three ridings that are close to me in northern Ontario, the ridings of Cochrane, Timmins and Timis-kaming, there is not one winter works scheme so far as I have been able to ascertain; absolutely none. There cannot be any winter works program, because of the manner in which this scheme is constituted. I would suggest that this fact be given some consideration. It is time that these northern municipalities were able to enjoy the benefits of legislation, just as the municipalities in other parts of Canada are able to do.
In the first place, under this winter works program the federal government pays only for labour. We have found that even if the period of time for this program were extended and there were not four or five feet of frost in the ground or very close to 150 inches of snow on the ground, we would still only be able to employ a very small labour force. We have been told that by the time the municipality employs the foremen, and the people who are specialists in their field, the actual labour force would be only four or five at the outside. If the labour costs was 10 per cent in connection with that project, the federal government would only have to assist with 5 per cent of the total cost of that project.
As everyone in Canada knows, the municipalities are experiencing considerable difficulty in obtaining money for sewers, roadbuilding and other jobs of that nature because of the high interest rates on the moneys that they have to borrow. The winter works program in my part of the country, therefore, and I think this is true of many more areas, has no effect at all. I agree the municipalities need this particular program. A suggestion was made by the hon. member for Timmins that we might extend this program a month at both ends of the period and this might, in some cases, allow some of the municipalities to take advantage of it.
Another very important problem in connection with unemployment is the kind of unemployment against which you cannot insure. I refer to area unemployment. This area unemployment is almost equal from coast to coast. We attempted last week to introduce a resolution which would have allowed discussion of this problem in terms of the unemployment in such areas as Cape

Breton island, Pictou county which has been mentioned this afternoon, Sable river in British Columbia, Bancroft, Elliot Lake and other areas. This is a problem in my own area. We have a large woodworking plant which because of conditions beyond their control is no longer able to employ the 500 people it used to employ and is now employing only five or six. This is a situation which we find throughout the railway industry where automation and other conditions have caused a cut-back in employment. This is the type of unemployment against which the worker cannot insure. This area displacement in many cases becomes a direct responsibility of the government. I should like particularly to discuss this area unemployment problem in terms of one particular area with which I am quite familiar, namely the Elliot Lake area.
This obviously is a government responsibility. This area of unemployment certainly is the baby of the federal government and the provincial government concerned and has been discussed in one way or another in the various aspects of the problem. In Elliot Lake we have a community that was started for one purpose. It is as well put in an article written by Larry Sefton as by any. He points out as follows:
The uranium industry owes its life to state research and it was financed by state investment-
He goes on to say:
-has depended almost entirely upon government planning and government expenditure-
Then he goes on to point out:
Research, development, and production of atomic energy has been a product of public, not private, enterprise.
This is one case where the government has had something to do with an area which is now going to be totally unemployed. We read headlines to the effect that there will be 3,000 workers out of work and others which indicate that the number will be 4,000. I would suggest that not only are 3,000 or 4,000 people going to be out of work but that a community of 25,000 people is going to be in this unemployment position owing to area unemployment.
The Liberal government has had some responsibility. Very recently in this house we had a debate in which the leader of the Liberal party pointed out what had been done and how the situation arose in the first place. He then went on to say what the government had not done in this particular case. What he said was true. What he said applied to the government. But I would suggest that it applied much more to him and to his party than it did to the present government with respect to this particular area.

Let it be remembered, Mr. Chairman, that there is not much difference between the unemployment situation at Elliot Lake and the situation that developed in area unemployment a short time ago in connection with the Avro Arrow project. You will remember that at that time, as in this case, planning was not developed to the stage where any future was assured to those workers simply because the work had not been done in planning for this particular area.
If this was an ordinary mining community, you would say that might have been expected. But the province of Ontario, because of conditions existing, did not allow the miners to go into Elliot Lake as they normally do. I know this from past experience because I have been involved. A miner normally going into a development area goes into that area with the idea of either working in the development stages of the area and getting out-staying only as long as the large money is to be made-or he goes in there to make a living for himself. In most cases, in most mining communities-and you can go back to Cobalt, Timmins, Kirkland Lake and the others-these communities began with tarpaper shacks. You hear stories of banks being installed in camps, a restaurant being run in a circus tent and so on. However, in Elliot Lake the Ontario planning board went in and said, "This town must meet specific conditions" and the town was built in that way. It was built with $40 million of our money from Ottawa through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and it was built with a great number of millions of dollars from the Ontario government for the development of sewers and streets. I would ask you to remember, Mr. Chairman, that this town has no unpaved streets. It is probably the only city of 25,000 in which all the streets are paved. It was built for the future and that future was a very flimsy one.
The Leader of the Opposition last night said that in signing a five-year agreement for the contracts for this production and in bringing this production into being they thought they were doing a service to that industry. It is also true that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation knew this industry was not going to last under that type of contract and they said, "We will go in here only for five years and from then on the C.M.H.C. mortgages must be carried by the companies themselves". Hence they did not take any chance.
I have many friends

many people with whom I have worked-who went into this area of Elliot Lake. They went in there to work. I advised many of them, fellows with whom I worked who went in at the development stage, to make sure not to buy a house
Supply-Labour
there and not to consider it as a permanent settlement. They must have known there was going to be trouble when the contracts ran out in 1962. They knew they could not be renewed.
To be fair about it, it was not known that they were not going to be renewed. We had been told that uranium was going to be in short supply across the world. But we knew when these mines were brought into production, having regard to the size of them, there would be the same problem, we expected, as in gold where we had a surplus of the commodity and the price would be far lower than we could afford to sell it at; in other words, the mines would not be able to produce at the price they would get for their product. That is not what has happened. We cannot sell this stuff. We cannot give it away at the present time.
When the present government says that the responsibility is that of the former government, I think that is true. I think we must now stop trying to decide whose fault it was and devote our attention to what we are going to do about the situation. I would suggest that the present government has done nothing about it. That is why I think this area unemployment problem is one that this government must face now. It is not good enough to say that what was done previously was not satisfactory.
We have this community; we have a permanent community at Elliot Lake and something can be done for that community if this government wants to give leadership. I would suggest that some of my miner friends working in Elliot Lake have put a great deal of money into homes and a great deal of money into that community. Indeed, some of them are now resting in the graveyard in that area because the development of this uranium industry cost 57 lives. Some of those 57 people have made a permanent contribution to that community. I think the other people have a right to ask that something be done now for this community and I think this government is the one that is going to have to do it.
In listening to the minister speaking last night on this problem, I was greatly surprised to find that he derived any satisfaction out of the fact that he was able to extend these contracts. This is no answer. This community cannot exist if you take away three quarters of the money that is coming in. The storekeepers will go broke, as will the people that went in and established a hospital and others who are involved. For instance, I have a friend who owns a dental clinic up there and who spent $80,000 or $90,000. This undertaking will not be able to exist if there are only 6,000 or 7,000 people

Supply-Labour
there. It can be carried on only in an expanding community. They were looking toward the future, not looking into the past. I suggest this has been no solution and will be no solution for these people; and I think they will be quite happy to come and tell the government that this is no solution to that particular problem.
I use Elliot Lake only as an example. I am sure that, if he wished to do so, the hon. member who represents the riding in which Sable river is situated, could rise in his place and tell you exactly the same story in his community. I am quite sure the representatives from Cape Breton island and Pictou county could rise in their places and tell you that in their area something must be done. I suggest that before I finish they will probably agree that it must be done by this government and that it must be done somewhat along the lines that I hope to suggest.
This problem of depression areas is not new to governments and it is not new to mining. It has always been there in the north and very little has been done about it.
The former government for reasons known to themselves decided that they would save the gold mining industry by passing the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. But this act has not saved those communities and it cannot be the answer even if it were made a permanent act. It is only a stopgap to carry us over until they decide what to do to supplement the income, because no matter what you do, a mine will eventually be worked out anyway. So if we were honest in passing the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act in the first place, we must carry through and develop something to supplant it.
In other countries they have used various methods to overcome this problem. We in Canada find that industrial development has to follow population, and I think if free enterprise is left on its own it will follow population. We have seen almost all the industry in the province of Ontario centered in the Toronto area. I suggest this is not a good employment practice for a country to observe. I think we could get much more benefit as Canadians if we were to decentralize a lot of this industrial development which is now causing such havoc in the city of Toronto and its surrounding areas where workers have to get on a street car two hours before they are due to start work in order to reach there on time.
This raises another problem in the employment picture. People were laid off in large numbers on the Avro Arrow project, and I think this problem rests squarely on

the shoulders of the present government because they blamed the previous government for doing it but they did nothing about it themselves except to stop the development. They did not do anything about the unemployed people, many of whom are still unemployed. In the city of Toronto they were able to get jobs in various parts of the city, and the problem never remained as apparent as it is in northern Ontario. These miners who are laid off in northern Ontario have no place to go. I know of no major mining development taking place in Canada today which would employ any number of miners. This is not the pattern Which has existed over the years, because I can remember when it was Belle Isle, when it was Yellowknife, when it was Uranium City, Knob Lake, Sudbury, and then Elliot Lake. Always before there has been some place for miners to go, but now I know of no place where they can go.
I should like to make some positive suggestions. All sorts of statements have been made; everybody blames everybody else, which I think is a good thing. I think -that has to be done and the Conservatives have to be able to say that the Liberals did it, and I think the Liberals have to be able to say the Conservatives did it. But I think that we as members of parliament have to speak for these people in Elliot Lake and forget the reason and ask ourselves, where do we go from here? I have a long article here which will interest the people of Elliot Lake. I do not want to read it all, but it is an editorial in the Sudbury Star, which incidentally is the newspaper which serves Elliot Lake. The headline is, "Was Elliot Lake dropped to satisfy the political situation in Manitoba?" Then it goes on to say:
Trade minister Churchill is from Winnipeg South Centre.
Prime Minister Diefenbaker is from the west.
Premier Roblin of Manitoba is chairman of the Manitoba development authority which has been working in close liaison with Atomic Energy of Canada Limited . ..
It is fair speculation that there may be political overtones because Liberal leader Pearson's riding is Algoma East, in which Elliot Lake is located.
True, these points may be evaded by Ottawa as "political guesswork," but they appear to be more pertinent than trade minister Churchill's talk about "national interest". The general political palatibility of distributing "gifts" from one end of the country to the other, regardless of other factors, is "smart politics" but sometimes unsound in the true national interest.
I am not suggesting this editorial is true. I am not suggesting that the minister did this, although I would not put it past governments to do this because it has been done in the past. Frankly, I do not think it is too important if we move this particular project at White Shell to Elliot Lake as far as the

employment situation is concerned, tor the simple reason that very few miners will work there because of their training. Therefore I do not think that necessarily this is the industry we need in that particular area. But everyone knows we need industry, and I suggest that this government should give fairly close consideration to setting up a manpower resources board.
Let me first of all point out that I do not want this manpower resources board to be the one which was established during the war as a war measure, because the main fault with that board was that once a man was placed in a job he could not get out of that job even if he wished. I want the manpower board to assess the field of availability under the direction of the unemployment insurance commission. They have been singularly unsuccessful, in the main, in being able to find places for workers. I think the reason is that they have not been able to make on an over-all basis a clear enough assessment of what are the needs. When they assess the needs, then they have to have the facilities and the money to re-train and re-locate people in jobs which these people are willing to accept.
This government and other governments will from now on have to give really close consideration to using our working force in the best possible national interest, and will have to give some assistance in this regard. I think the companies, particularly the mining companies, should help. I can show where $25 million was invested in Rio Tinto, which would make them a very large sum of money under the terms of their contract. If that mine had existed for another five or ten years they would have made a mint of money, enough to run this country, if they could have operated without any expenses, as they have.
It has been drawn to my attention that Bob Winters is president of that company, so the Liberal government is very close to the situation and the Leader of the Opposition should be able to give first-hand information on this. Also, he had quite a bit to do with this in days gone by and is or was a director of the board of that particular company.
I think other things can also be done by the manpower resources board. I think we can demand that mines in development areas must have a reason for existence. We would have been a lot better off if not one ton of uranium had ever been mined at Elliot Lake. We would have been much better off if that community had never been born, because it is now costing our national income a lot of money because there is an industry there which we have to assume responsibility for whether we like it or not. We established that industry only to satisfy the United States.

I say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce who is here today that we have paid very dearly for our deal with the United States, and I demand that he consider very closely curtailing any further support for the defences of the United States until they put some money into helping run the industry which they caused us to create, in order to keep these peonle working in that industry. They were responsible for this and it is a two-way street; if it is not we had better get off it because we are getting the short end of that particular deal.
I suggest that we curtail our assistance to their defences till we get some defence for our own industries which we built for the defence of all America. That is the only justification we had for ever going into this uranium deal, because I think the minister indicated last night that it will be a long time past 1970 before we will be using very much uranium for industrial purposes.
I think this board should also have the right to assess pension plans, and to demand from industries of this nature severance pay. I know that this severance pay which has been negotiated by the unions at Elliot Lake is going to be considered by the minister. The minister cannot ignore the fact that here is an opportunity to help these miners in their resettlement problems and I think that this is one small way in which his department has the opportunity to do something about this.

subtopic: MINDEN, ONT.  PETITION CONCERNING ANGUS COULTER
speechtext:
I believe we should give close consideration to ascertaining what measure of decentralization can take place in our industry. Certainly, good places for consideration are the areas affected at the present time, particularly the mining areas. I think something else should be done, namely the setting up of a national industrial planning board. One of the measures which would help solve this problem would be the development of secondary industries, and I suggest that a board could be set up to assist in such development. It may be that the committee is not too familiar with the inducement offered to mining undertakings, but if secondary industry were given the same advantages as mining companies, many smaller firms might be induced to come to an area such as Elliot Lake.
It should be remembered that Elliot Lake is only a few hours drive from Sault Ste. Marie and that it can be reached after an overnight drive from the city of Toronto. It takes no more than 12 hours to get to Montreal. Many of these areas of northern Ontario which have developed as mining areas and which are not now finding it economical to continue could be advantageously changed into industrial areas if the government were to set up a board to examine the potentialities in those areas and then offer inducements in order to bring in secondary industry.
In the mining areas mines going into production are given a three-year tax exemption period. If we offered the same advantage to secondary industry many of these smaller secondary plants which are being built in
major cities at the present time might well be attracted elsewhere, especially if we pointed out that they would be moving into communities where there was a complete range of services including sewers, water, schools, fire halls and so on and where the federal government had speeded up amortization to the mining companies bringing new mines into development.
Such a board as I was suggesting was established in the United Kingdom not long ago and certain inducements were offered to industry to go into areas where labour was available or where natural resources were available. If we follow this example I think we could help solve this problem.
I do hope that we can take Elliot Lake out of the political arena and put it back in the employment field. I have worked in that area. I was in there when there were only sawmills in that area. We have a beautiful little city there of 25,000 inhabitants-hardworking people who want to settle down. Some of them have been there for three or four years, and their children are attending schools in that area. I think all the Canadian people will wish to retain that community as it is. We cannot, of course, retain all the miners, but with some help a proportion, at least, of the working force could be retained. Those who can remain will be a credit to Canada if they are only given the help they need; the help which, I suggest, should be given by this government.
Progress reported.
I wonder if I could ask the leader of the house what the plans are for the remainder of the week and if there has been any change from the program announced yesterday.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I regret that I cannot say tonight what the order will be on Friday, because there may be one or two changes. However, I can be sure of this for Friday- a continuation of supplementary estimates and the resolution standing in the name of the Minister of Public Works dealing with the amendments to the National Housing Act. By tomorrow night I may be able to add one or two items to that if the house will give me some assurance that it requires more business for Friday.
At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.﻿FEBRUARY 24, 1960
